coffee-latte-decaffeinated-with-non-dair.title: Decaf Latte with Non-Dairy Milk, Flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Decaf latte is a coffee‑based drink in which the caffeine has been removed, combined with a generous amount of frothed non‑dairy milk (soy, oat, almond, etc.) and flavorings such as vanilla, caramel, or nut extracts. It retains the creamy character of a classic latte while containing virtually no caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water, carbon‑dioxide or solvent methods, preserving most of the coffee’s flavor compounds.
Plant‑based milks contain less saturated fat than cow’s milk and are suitable for vegans.
Flavored versions often use natural extracts, though some may contain artificial flavorings.
Decaf latte is popular among caffeine‑sensitive individuals, pregnant women, and children.
In several countries decaffeinated coffee is classified as a separate product category with its own regulations.

items.title: Reduced nervous system stimulation
items.content: The lack of caffeine lowers the risk of anxiety, insomnia, and rapid heart rate.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Decaf coffee retains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Gentler on the stomach
items.content: Without caffeine, the drink is less likely to irritate the gastric lining.

items.title: Low sugar content (when unsweetened)
items.content: If no sweetener is added, the beverage contains virtually no sugar, supporting blood‑glucose control.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals from plant milk
items.content: Soy and oat milks are often fortified with calcium, vitamin D, and B12.

items.title: Allergy to plant ingredients
items.content: Soy, almond, or oat milks can trigger allergic reactions in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Some flavorings may contain artificial sweeteners or preservatives that not everyone tolerates.

items.title: Possible flavor loss during decaffeination
items.content: The decaffeination process can diminish the intensity of coffee flavor compared with regular latte.

content.title: How to Enjoy
content.content: Serve hot or iced, optionally adding a sweetener, a sprinkle of cinnamon, or cocoa powder. It can also be used as a base for dessert cocktails, smoothies, or incorporated into baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared drink refrigerated and consume within 24 hours. Store dry ingredients (coffee granules, flavorings) in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place.

hamburger-on-wheat-bun-1-large-patty.title: Hamburger on Wheat Bun with Large Patty

content.title: About
content.content: A hamburger is a classic fast‑food item consisting of a large beef patty (about 170 g) placed between a split wheat bun. It is often served with lettuce, tomato, onion, pickles, cheese, and various sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first hamburger was served in the United States in the late 19th century.
A wheat bun gives a soft texture and a mild grain flavor compared with rye buns.
A 170 g patty is considered a “premium‑size” and is common in upscale fast‑food chains.
The hamburger has become an icon of American culture and is popular worldwide.
There are over 300 variations of toppings and sauces, ranging from classic to exotic.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: The beef patty provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of iron
items.content: Red meat contains heme iron, which is more readily absorbed than plant‑based iron.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Hamburgers supply vitamins B12, B6, and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: The wheat bun offers complex carbs that provide sustained energy.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If made with whole‑grain flour, the bun adds fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: A large patty and bun make the hamburger calorie‑dense; moderation is key for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Beef contains saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels when consumed in excess.

items.title: Salt and sauces
items.content: Sauces often add significant sodium and sugar, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The wheat bun contains gluten, unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hamburgers are typically eaten by hand, holding the bun so the patty and toppings stay in place. Add fresh vegetables, cheese, avocado, or swap heavy sauces for lighter options.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared hamburger in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. For longer storage, separate the bun and patty, wrap each in airtight containers, and reheat the patty to an internal temperature of 71 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Marie biscuit is a light, dry biscuit originally created in the United Kingdom in 1874. It has a delicate buttery flavor, crisp texture, and a characteristic square shape. The biscuit is often enjoyed as a simple snack, with tea or milk, and is also used in desserts.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original Marie biscuit was named after Princess Marie, daughter of King Edward VII.
It quickly became popular in the Soviet Union, where it was a staple in school cafeterias.
The classic recipe uses wheat flour, vegetable oil, sugar, and a leavening agent.
Marie biscuits are frequently used as a base for "torte" and cheesecake recipes.
In some countries the biscuit is sold under different brand names but retains the same formula.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Marie biscuits contain a modest amount of fat, making them suitable for moderate consumption in low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The carbohydrates provide quick energy, useful for a light snack.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Small amounts of vitamins B1 and B2 support normal metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: The soft texture allows rapid digestion without heavy stomach load.

items.title: Kid‑friendly
items.content: Small size and mild texture make the biscuit convenient for children (when no allergy is present).

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Marie biscuits contain sugar, so people with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Made with wheat flour, the biscuit is not suitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Allergy to additives
items.content: Some versions may contain flavorings or preservatives that could trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Marie biscuits can be eaten plain, dipped in tea, milk, or coffee. They are often used in desserts: crushed for a cake base, added to ice cream, or prepared as a milk‑pudding.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the biscuits in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.
